newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - NZ's Evergreen plans to double estate.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - NZ's Evergreen plans to double estate.

text.p: Evergreen Forests Ltd expects to double its forest estate to around 30,000 hectares within one to three years and is not far away from an acquisition, Chief Executive Mark Bogle said in an interview on Wednesday.
Any substantial purchase would require an injection of equity, he added.
"We are actively looking at several properties and I would be disappointed if something could not be consummated soon," he said, adding he expected this to happen before mid-1997.

Evergreen was formed in 1993 with market capitalisation of NZ$23 million to invest directly in plantation forestry through acquisition of existing forests and through the purchase of land for new plantings. From an initial estate of 1,000 hectares the company now has 14,000 ha.
Bogle said the maturity profile of the existing forests was not ideal, with an average age of 16 years compared to the normal harvest age of 28 years.
"Although we've expanded 14 times, we have not got a 14 times greater asset base because the value of younger trees is very much less than trees nearer to harvest," he said.
Evergreen nevertheless had significant areas coming up for harvest in two years time.

"But we are really only part way there. We are looking to expand aggressively still from where we are. The ultimate profile of the company will be more determined by what we acquire from now on, than what we own at present," he said.

"By going to 30,000 ha we are not just talking about doubling our asset base. By improving our maturity profile we are going to have to acquire more valuable, older forests, so I would say this would achieve that critical mass," he said.
Evergreen had identified institutions that would be keen to participate in the company's next growth phase.
Growth to date had been enhanced by a NZ$50 million capital injection from its 60 percent owner, U.S. based pension fund Xylem Investments.

Bogle said there were opportunities apparent in Fletcher Forest's decision to sell down its interests outside the central North Island but Fletcher's Hikurangi estate, on the east coast of the North Island, would be too big to swallow.
However, it was a forest that Evergreen could participate in jointly, similar to the way Forestry Corp of NZ was sold to FCL, Brierley Investments and China's Citic.
But Evergreen was more likely to focus on small to medium sized forests of between 1,000 to 4,000 hectares, which make up some 400,000 hectares of New Zealand's total forest estate.
Evergreen's share price traded on Wednesday at NZ$0.61 against estimates of net asset value of NZ$0.80, and the stock has struggled to perform since its inception.
Bogle said the share price was constrained by its small market capitalisation, a lack of liquidity caused by Xylem's large holding and the company's low cash flow profile.
Bogle said Xylem was supportive of Evergreen's goals, one of which was to broaden the shareholder base. Xylem, he said, was not "wedded" to the controlling stake.
